title: What makes an adventure film memorable

commenti.body: Obviously having awesome setpieces helps, but I think having lovable memorable characters is even more important. If you don't care about the cast then an awesome setpiece won't save the movie.

The same thing that makes many films memorable. Characters that feel real to the audience and stakes that feel real to the characters. Caring about the characters and their mission/quest/journey/arc/etc obviously takes us from being kinda invested to being very invested.

As far as keeping action and setpieces at a lower budget... I don't really know. You'll have to find some spot between "blockbuster CGI-fest" and "LARPing in the woods".  
I guess interesting real locations are gonna beat mystical fake locations in that regard.

I was playing Uncharted 4: A Thief's End and it got me thinking about how it would be a great adventure film, the kind they don't make anymore unless it's yet another Indiana Jones flop. The game is more along the lines of Romancing The Stone I think. Action set pieces are one thing, but what a good movie really needs is a cast of great characters, beautiful locales and imaginative set design.

I think one of the challenges with an adventure film is that it typically involves some sort of travel - you have to go on an adventure after all. You can manage action films on a relatively low budget - take something like Hot Fuzz. It only has one action sequence that involves a significant budget, most of the strength of it is in the script and chemistry of the cast. You can keep the budget relatively low because the scale of the action is limited to a village and the main action is on the high street and in the supermarket. It works though, because it's shot like an action movie, so even though the scale and stakes are small, they're shot seriously (even though it's a comedy).

Another avenue for adventure is to make the adventure exist in the character's imaginations. Swallows and Amazons is a book about kids on a summer holiday in the Lake District where they go to camp on an island. But they imagine everything as part of the classic adventure stories like Treasure Island. The adventure is primarily a competition between them and the Amazons, a local pair of sisters who have similar imaginations. But in the 1974 adaptation none of the visuals are modified to appear anything other than they are, but their imagination comes through in the sound. It's a great adventure film, but also pretty low budget.

The main challenge to budget in an adventure film is not the set pieces, you have to forgo those. But in figuring out a scope that can be implemented on that budget. A witty script, a good cast, and a story that feels like it matters to the characters are most important. You probably can't have a 'save the world' scale - but those stories don't necessarily matter that much. The smaller the stakes, sometimes, the more the audience cares because they know the world won't end, but they don't know that something smaller won't go wrong.
